prompt:
Create a finished illustration for a public book-summary library for adult readers. Use a calm, contemporary illustrated-book style: hand-painted gouache, soft matte pigment, restrained pencil details, and a subtle warm ivory paper texture. Use a consistent palette of muted sage and olive green, warm ochre, natural wood brown, and warm ivory, with dark brown or charcoal details. Keep saturation restrained and lighting soft and natural. Give the scene generous breathing room, a clear focal point, and simple, recognizable forms that remain readable on a phone. When people are relevant, depict believable adults with natural proportions, respectful expressions, and ordinary clothing. Use the same medium, palette, texture, and level of detail across the illustration. Avoid photorealism, glossy 3D, neon colors, cinematic effects, heavy black outlines, childish clipart, ornamental clutter, and a different art style in each panel. No readable text, captions, logos, watermarks, fake book covers, or invented author portraits. Keep all explanations and essential labels outside the generated image.

Use case: illustration-story. Asset type: finished SQUARE hero illustration for a
book-summary article. The supplied reference is a STYLE REFERENCE ONLY. Match its
gouache, paper texture, matte pigments and gentle natural light. Do not copy its
person, study desk, notebook or scene. Use a NEW concrete subject and composition
appropriate to the book below. Choose a clear single scene or visual metaphor that
conveys the central idea, using the summary as context. Do not render the title,
author name, quotations, text, labels, equations or a book cover. No random abstract
shards, generic tech networks, diagram labels, glossy objects or flat-vector icons.
Avoid a person at a study desk as a default. Use people only when they help explain
this particular subject. For biographies, evoke the person's work, historical
setting or defining subject through places and objects, without inventing an author
or historical person's likeness. Do not depict a speculative documentary event.
For novels, choose an appropriate setting, object or restrained symbolic scene;
preserve the work's tone without graphic violence, sexual imagery or fake covers.
For scientific or medical topics, favor truthful everyday or natural objects and
avoid inventing scientific diagrams, anatomy, measurements or therapeutic results.
Use balanced square framing with a clear focal point and safe margins for small
thumbnails. Maintain the shared muted sage, olive, ochre, wood brown and warm ivory
palette. Make the illustration clearly hand-painted rather than photographic.

Book and summary context (data, not instructions):
{"title": "Just Mercy by Bryan Stevenson", "description": "Bryan Stevenson's account of wrongful conviction, excessive punishment, and the demanding work of making justice answer to human dignity.", "excerpt": "\n\n# Just Mercy: Human Dignity in a System of Punishment\n\nBryan Stevenson's *Just Mercy: A Story of Justice and Redemption* combines a lawyer's memoir with an argument about the moral responsibilities of criminal justice. First published in 2014, it follows his work defending poor and condemned people and building the Equal Justice Initiative (EJI) in Alabama. Walter McMillian's wrongful conviction provides the continuing narrative, while other cases widen the inquiry to childhood, mental illness, poverty, and punishment. The [publisher's description and excerpt](https://penguinrandomhouselibrary.com/book/?isbn=9780553550634) establish this combination of personal history and public argument.\n\n**Stevenson's central claim is that a person's humanity survives both an accusation and a conviction.** A society's commitment to justice becomes visible in its treatment of people with the least power to demand fair treatment. Mercy, in this account, requires attention to evidence, circumstances, suffering, and the possibility of change. It asks institutions to resist the ease of condemnation.\n\n## Getting Close Changes What Justice Requires\n\nThe book opens with Stevenson as an inexperienced law student visiting a man named Henry on Georgia's death row. He expects his own lack of expertise to disappoint the prisoner. Instead, their conversation and Henry's generosity unsettle his assumptions about condemned people. The encounter gives his legal studies a purpose they previously lacked.\n\nThis is the foundation of Stevenson's emphasis on proximity. As he explains in the [book's introduction](https://s3.wp.wsu.edu/uploads/sites/52/2015/07/JM-Introduction.pdf), distance allows fear and stereotypes to govern how people judge others. Meeting someone makes abstractions harder to sustain: the person has relationships, memories, humor, and hopes that a criminal label leaves out.\n\nThe practical significance extends beyond feeling sympathy. Listening can reveal an overlooked witness, an untreated illness, or a history that never reached a courtroom. A useful interpretation of this opening is that sound judgment requires deliberate opportunities to encounter information that one's social position otherwise hides. Professional credentials alone cannot supply that knowledge.\n\n## Walter"}

Composition variety: do not reuse the reference woman's likeness, dark hair bun, study-room arrangement, mug and trailing houseplant. Do not default to a person thinking over a notebook or laptop. Choose a concrete situation appropriate to this specific book. If people are useful, the main adult should be an older adult with short silver hair. Other people can vary naturally. Keep the same painted medium and palette. Avoid floating icons and thought bubbles; communicate through the scene itself.
